messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 78
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Environmental Scientist
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 70

# The Weight of Responsibility

Dr. Khalil sits in the leather chair across from me, his posture still bearing the careful dignity of someone accustomed to precision and control. At seventy-eight, his face carries the lines of a man who has spent a lifetime observing natural systems—studying soil composition, water quality, ecosystem dynamics. But there is something else etched into those lines now, something that emerged five years ago and has not left.

The accident happened on a Saturday morning in spring. Dr. Khalil had been conducting field research at a local nature preserve for nearly forty years, monitoring the same plots of land through seasons of change. He knew every path, every geological feature. That morning, he was driving the research vehicle down a narrow access road, moving slowly as he always did, when a young graduate student suddenly stepped into the path from behind a thick stand of trees. There was no time. The impact was immediate and catastrophic.

The student—a twenty-three-year-old named Marcus—suffered a shattered femur and multiple internal injuries. He spent three weeks in intensive care. He survived, but the recovery has been long and incomplete. Marcus walks with a permanent limp now. He did not return to finish his degree.

Dr. Khalil was not cited. The accident investigation concluded it was unavoidable. The student had been in a restricted area, distracted, moving unpredictably. By every measure of culpability, Dr. Khalil was blameless. But he does not feel blameless. He feels like a man who set something terrible in motion, and no amount of external exoneration has altered that internal reality.

For the first two years, Dr. Khalil tried to continue his work. But the research site had become impossible. He would arrive at the preserve and feel his chest tighten. His hands would shake when holding equipment. The familiar landscape that had once brought him peace now triggered an overwhelming sense of dread. He retired early, something he had never planned to do.

At home, his wife notices that he startles at sudden sounds—car doors closing, the telephone ringing. He will be reading the newspaper and suddenly his mind will produce the image of Marcus's face in the moment after impact, though he was not actually looking at the student's face then. His sleep is fragmented. He wakes at three or four in the morning and cannot return to sleep, his mind cycling through variations of what might have happened differently.

He has begun avoiding driving altogether, which troubles him deeply. A man who prided himself on careful observation and risk assessment now feels unsafe behind the wheel. His wife drives them everywhere now. He knows this is irrational—he was not at fault, the conditions were unavoidable—but knowing this intellectually has done nothing to quiet the conviction in his body that he cannot be trusted with such responsibility.

What haunts him most is the uncertainty about Marcus's life now. He has thought about reaching out many times but has not. What would he say? The guilt feels like it belongs to him, and any contact feels like an attempt to transfer it, to make Marcus absolve him. So he carries it alone, in the early morning hours when sleep will not come, in the way his hands still tremble slightly when he thinks about that spring morning.

His wife urged him to seek help, and after years of resistance, he finally agreed. He sits here now, a man of science accustomed to measurable data, trying to articulate something that feels immeasurable and endless.
